nodes.label: Süleyman I
nodes.full: Süleyman, known in Turkish as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, took Belgrade in 1521, Rhodes in 1522, most of Hungary after Mohács in 1526 and Baghdad in 1534, and in his 46-year reign carried the empire to its widest extent in Europe; he died on campaign at Szigetvár in 1566. He executed two of his sons, Mustafa in 1553 and Bayezid in 1561, and the succession passed to Selim II.
nodes.src: Halil İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age (1973); Metin Kunt and Christine Woodhead (eds.), Süleyman the Magnificent and His Age (1995); Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002).

nodes.label: Hürrem Sultan
nodes.full: Hürrem (Roxelana), a slave from Ruthenia, became Süleyman's favourite and, against precedent, his legal wife in about 1533–1534; she bore him several sons, including the future Selim II, corresponded with the king of Poland and the Safavid shah, built a mosque complex in Istanbul and a charity at Jerusalem, and was credited by contemporaries and later writers with the fall of the grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha in 1536 and of Prince Mustafa in 1553.
nodes.src: Leslie Peirce, The Imperial Harem (1993); Ottoman and Venetian ambassadors' reports (Bassano; relazioni).

nodes.label: Sokollu Mehmed Pasha
nodes.full: Sokollu, a Bosnian taken by the devshirme, was grand vizier under Süleyman, Selim II and Murad III and ran the empire in the years after Szigetvár, restoring the fleet after Lepanto in a winter, planning a Don–Volga canal and a Suez canal, building mosques and waterworks and making peace with the emperor; he was stabbed by a soldier in 1579.
nodes.src: Imber 2002; Kunt and Woodhead 1995; İnalcık 1973.

nodes.label: Selim II and Murad III
nodes.full: Selim II, who did not go on campaign, ruled from 1566 to 1574 through Sokollu and Joseph Nasi and took Cyprus in 1570–1571; Murad III (1574–1595), who never took the field at the head of his army, lived in the harem, where his mother Nurbanu and his favourite Safiye had great influence, and was succeeded by his son Mehmed III, who killed 19 brothers on his accession.
nodes.src: Imber 2002; Leslie Peirce 1993; Baki Tezcan, The Second Ottoman Empire (2010).

nodes.label: Ahmed I
nodes.full: Ahmed I, who came to the throne at 13 and did not kill his brother Mustafa, kept him confined in the palace, beginning a new practice: from his time the princes, who had once governed provinces, were housed in the Kafes, the cage, and succession went to the eldest male of the dynasty. His reign saw the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, the peace of Zsitvatorok and the Safavid war.
nodes.src: Peirce 1993; Tezcan 2010; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Osman II and Murad IV
nodes.full: Osman II, aged 14 at his accession, was deposed and strangled by Janissaries in May 1622, after his failure at Khotin and his plan to reform the corps, the first time a sultan was murdered by his own troops; Murad IV (1623–1640) came to the throne at 11, ended the rule of the mothers and the army, put down the rebellions with terror, banned coffee and tobacco in the capital and took Baghdad from the Safavids in 1638.
nodes.src: Tezcan 2010; Naima, Tarih; Katip Çelebi, Fezleke; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Kösem Sultan
nodes.full: Kösem, a Greek slave in the harem of Ahmed I, was queen mother and regent for her sons Murad IV and Ibrahim and for her grandson Mehmed IV; she influenced appointments for decades and was strangled in September 1651 by the party of her rival, the young sultan's mother Turhan Hatice. The period is called the sultanate of women in the older literature.
nodes.src: Peirce 1993; Naima; Tezcan 2010.

nodes.label: The Köprülüs
nodes.full: In 1656, at the height of a military and financial crisis, the queen mother Turhan Hatice gave full powers to Köprülü Mehmed Pasha, an Albanian official of 80, who put down opponents, restored discipline and recovered the Dardanelles from the Venetians; his son Fazıl Ahmed (1661–1676), who took Crete and Podolia, and Kara Mustafa (1676–1683), who led the army to Vienna, kept the office in the family.
nodes.src: Naima; Rhoads Murphey, Ottoman Warfare 1500–1700 (1999); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Ibrahim and Mehmed IV
nodes.full: Ibrahim, a sultan with a reputation for excess, was deposed and strangled in 1648 after years of financial crisis and the war in Crete, and his son Mehmed IV, who came to the throne at six, ruled until 1687 under his mother and the Köprülüs, spending most of the time at Edirne for the hunt; his reign saw the greatest territorial extent of the empire and the failure at Vienna.
nodes.src: Naima; Imber 2002; Abou-El-Haj, The 1703 Rebellion (1984).

nodes.label: Mohács
nodes.full: Süleyman's army with some 60,000 men and 160 guns destroyed the Hungarian force of Louis II in two hours at Mohács on the Danube; the king drowned and the kingdom split between Ferdinand of Habsburg and John Zápolya, an Ottoman vassal, and Buda was occupied in 1541, beginning 150 years of Ottoman rule in central Hungary.
nodes.src: Kemal Pashazade, Tevarih-i Al-i Osman; Imber 2002; Géza Dávid and Pál Fodor (eds.), Ottomans, Hungarians, and Habsburgs (2000).

nodes.label: First siege of Vienna
nodes.full: Süleyman's army, held back by rain, lack of heavy guns and the early onset of winter, besieged the Habsburg capital for about three weeks and withdrew; the siege showed the practical limit of the army's reach from Istanbul and confirmed Vienna as the frontier of the Habsburg world.
nodes.src: Imber 2002; Murphey 1999; Dávid and Fodor 2000.

nodes.label: Preveza
nodes.full: Hayreddin Barbarossa, the Algerian corsair made admiral of the Ottoman fleet, with some 120 galleys defeated a Holy League fleet under Andrea Doria off Preveza; the victory gave the Ottomans control of the eastern and central Mediterranean for three decades and made Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli bases of Ottoman sea power.
nodes.src: Seyyid Murad, Gazavat-ı Hayreddin Paşa; Palmira Brummett, Ottoman Seapower and Levantine Diplomacy (1994); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Great Siege of Malta
nodes.full: A fleet of some 180 ships under Mustafa Pasha and Piyale Pasha, with up to 30,000 men and the corsair Turgut Reis, besieged the Knights of St John under Jean de Valette for almost four months, took Fort St Elmo after heavy losses and failed to take Birgu and Senglea; the relief force from Sicily compelled a retreat, a rare defeat of the Ottoman amphibious power.
nodes.src: Francisco Balbi di Correggio, The Siege of Malta 1565; Ernle Bradford, The Great Siege (1961).

nodes.label: Cyprus and Lepanto
nodes.full: The Ottomans took Cyprus from Venice in 1570–1571, after the sack of Nicosia and the long siege of Famagusta whose commander Bragadin was flayed, and at Lepanto on 7 October 1571 the Holy League's fleet under Don John of Austria destroyed most of the Ottoman galleys; the fleet was rebuilt within a year and the island was kept, so the battle changed little of the balance beyond the loss of many trained seamen.
nodes.src: Imber 2002; Brummett 1994; Andrew Hess, ‘The Battle of Lepanto and Its Place in Mediterranean History’, Past & Present 57 (1972).

nodes.label: Safavid wars and Amasya
nodes.full: Süleyman led three campaigns against Shah Tahmasp, took Baghdad in 1534 with its shrine of Abu Hanifa and the Shia cities of Najaf and Karbala, and gained Van and parts of the Caucasus; the Peace of Amasya of 1555 fixed a boundary between the empires that held, apart from the wars of 1578–1590 and 1603–1639, until the eighteenth century.
nodes.src: Matrakçı Nasuh, Beyan-ı Menazil-i Sefer-i Irakeyn; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Long Turkish War
nodes.full: A thirteen-year war between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs and their allies over Hungary and the Danube principalities, with the Ottoman capture of Eger in 1596 and the battle of Mezőkeresztes, was fought at the same time as the Jelali revolts; the Peace of Zsitvatorok in 1606 gave the emperor equality of title with the sultan and ended the tribute.
nodes.src: Treaty of Zsitvatorok (11 November 1606); Gábor Ágoston, Guns for the Sultan (2005); Murphey 1999.

nodes.label: Jelali revolts
nodes.full: Bands of unpaid soldiers, mercenary musketeers (sekban) and peasants, under leaders such as Karayazıcı, Deli Hasan and Canpulatoğlu, held large parts of Anatolia in the years of the Long War, burning villages and defeating government armies; many peasants fled the land and the countryside lost a part of its population, and the state recovered control only in about 1610.
nodes.src: William Griswold, The Great Anatolian Rebellion 1000–1020/1591–1611 (1983); Mustafa Akdağ, Celali İsyanları (1963).

nodes.label: Zuhab and Baghdad
nodes.full: Shah Abbas I recovered Tabriz and the Caucasus in 1603–1618 and took Baghdad in 1623, and Murad IV in 1638 besieged and retook the city; the treaty of Zuhab (Qasr-ı Şirin) of 1639 fixed the boundary of Iraq and eastern Anatolia more or less as it is today.
nodes.src: Treaty of Zuhab (1639); Matthee 2012; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Cretan war
nodes.full: The longest of the Ottoman–Venetian wars began with the landing at Chania and ended with the surrender of Candia (Heraklion) after a siege of 21 years, the longest in the history of the Mediterranean, by Fazıl Ahmed's army in September 1669; Venice kept a few fortresses, and the Ottomans held Crete until 1898.
nodes.src: Ellen Eickhoff, Venedig, Wien und die Osmanen (1970); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: St Gotthard
nodes.full: Fazıl Ahmed took the fortress of Neuhäusel (Érsekújvár) in 1663 and was checked at the Rába at St Gotthard on 1 August 1664 by a force of imperial, French and German troops under Raimondo Montecuccoli; the truce of Vasvár, twenty years long, gave the sultan more than he had won in the field.
nodes.src: Treaty of Vasvár (10 August 1664); Murphey 1999.

nodes.label: Second siege of Vienna
nodes.full: Kara Mustafa Pasha led an army of some 100,000 or more into Hungary, bypassed the fortresses on the way, and besieged the capital for two months; a relief army of Poles, Austrians and Germans under Jan III Sobieski and Charles of Lorraine attacked from the Kahlenberg on 12 September and broke the Ottoman camp. Kara Mustafa was executed at Belgrade in December, and the defeat began the Holy League's war and the retreat from central Europe.
nodes.src: Evliya Çelebi; Silahdar Findiklili Mehmed Ağa, Nusretname; John Stoye, The Siege of Vienna (1964).

nodes.label: Kanun and Ebussuud
nodes.full: Under Süleyman the provincial law codes, the kanunnames, were revised and the sultan's secular law was harmonised with the sharia by the chief mufti Ebussuud Efendi (şeyhülislam 1545–1574), who gave fatwas that justified the sultan's legislation, on land, taxes and crimes, in terms of the Hanafi law; the codification was the reason for the epithet Kanuni.
nodes.src: Colin Imber, Ebu's-su'ud: The Islamic Legal Tradition (1997); Uriel Heyd, Studies in Old Ottoman Criminal Law (1973).

nodes.label: The cage
nodes.full: After Mehmed III's execution of 19 brothers in 1595 and Ahmed I's refusal in 1603, princes were no longer sent to provinces and killed on the father's death but kept in the Kafes in the harem under guard, so that the heir often came to the throne with no experience of administration or war; seniority within the dynasty became the rule of succession by the 1620s–1640s.
nodes.src: Peirce 1993; Tezcan 2010; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Cadastre
nodes.full: The tahrir surveys of 1520–1580 recorded households, fields and dues in every province and fixed the timar system at its most developed; from the late sixteenth century the state, to pay for musketeers, converted many dues to cash and began leasing the revenue to tax farmers, so that the cavalry timar-holder became less important.
nodes.src: Ömer Lütfi Barkan, ‘Essai sur les données statistiques des registres de recensement’, JESHO 1 (1957); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Tax farming
nodes.full: Extraordinary levies, the avarız, once raised in wartime, became annual, and tax farming (iltizam) was extended from customs and mines to the provincial revenues, with life tenure introduced in the malikâne in 1695; the shift gave provincial notables a stake in the revenue and later the base of their power.
nodes.src: Linda Darling, Revenue-Raising and Legitimacy (1996); Metin Kunt, The Sultan's Servants (1983).

nodes.label: Divan and provinces
nodes.full: The Imperial Council of the viziers, the chief judges and the finance and chancery officers met in the Dome Room at Topkapı four days a week, while provinces were governed by beylerbeys, or governors, with a kadi and a financial officer in each; by the 1560s the empire had some twenty eyalets, among them Buda, Egypt, Damascus, Baghdad and the Islands.
nodes.src: İnalcık 1973; Imber 2002; Kunt 1983.

nodes.label: Capitulations
nodes.full: The privileges granted to French merchants, usually dated 1536 (a draft that may not have been ratified) and certainly renewed in 1569 and 1581, gave them security of trade and travel, freedom from local jurisdiction in civil cases, and consular courts, as acts of grace by the sultan; later extended to the English and the Dutch, they became in the nineteenth century a symbol of foreign privilege.
nodes.src: Halil İnalcık, ‘Imtiyāzāt’, EI2; Maurits van den Boogert, The Capitulations and the Ottoman Legal System (2005).

nodes.label: Sultan as caliph
nodes.full: After Selim I took Cairo and the keys of the Hijaz holy places, the sultan took the title Servant of the Two Holy Sanctuaries and, over time, the claim to the caliphate; the story of the last Abbasid caliph handing the office to Selim in 1517 is a later construct, and the claim was little used until the eighteenth century and revived by Abdülhamid II.
nodes.src: Imber 2002; İnalcık 1973; Selim Deringil, The Well-Protected Domains (1998).

nodes.label: Kadızadeli movement
nodes.full: The preacher Kadızade Mehmed (d. 1635) and his followers called for the removal of innovations such as the cult of saints, sufi music and dance, tobacco, coffee, and the veneration of tombs, and clashed with the Sufi orders for half a century, backed in the 1650s–1680s by Vani Mehmed Efendi; the movement was a form of Sunni revival and an expression of urban tensions.
nodes.src: Madeline Zilfi, ‘The Kadızadelis’, JNES 45 (1986); Katip Çelebi, Mizan ül-hakk (1656).

nodes.label: Shabbatai Zvi
nodes.full: Shabbatai Zvi, a kabbalist of Smyrna, was proclaimed the Messiah by Nathan of Gaza in 1665 and drew enthusiastic followers in Jewish communities from Amsterdam to Yemen; arrested in 1666 and brought before Mehmed IV at Edirne, he accepted Islam, and a group of his followers, the Dönme, continued as a secret sect in Salonica.
nodes.src: Gershom Scholem, Sabbatai Sevi: The Mystical Messiah (1973); Cengiz Şişman, The Burden of Silence (2015).

nodes.label: Joseph Nasi and Safed
nodes.full: Joseph Nasi, a Portuguese converso who returned to Judaism in Istanbul, became a favourite of Selim II, Duke of Naxos in 1566, and obtained from Süleyman a grant in 1561 to rebuild Tiberias and settle Jews there; Safed, with its printing press of 1577, the kabbalists Isaac Luria and Joseph Karo and its textile trade, became a centre of Jewish learning.
nodes.src: Cecil Roth, The House of Nasi (1948); Shaw, The Jews of the Ottoman Empire (1991).

nodes.label: Orthodox patriarchate
nodes.full: The Orthodox patriarchate under Ottoman rule, whose patriarchs were elected under pressure and often deposed, controlled its flock through the metropolitans and kept the Slavic churches under it after the abolition of the Serbian patriarchate in 1766; Cyril Lucaris, patriarch six times between 1612 and 1638, took Calvinist ideas and was strangled in 1638.
nodes.src: Steven Runciman, The Great Church in Captivity (1968); Braude and Lewis 1982.

nodes.label: Sinan and Süleymaniye
nodes.full: Mimar Sinan, a devshirme recruit who became chief architect in 1538 and built or supervised some 300 buildings, built the Şehzade (1548), the Süleymaniye (1550–1557) on the hill above the Golden Horn, with its dome of 27 metres and four minarets, and the Selimiye at Edirne (1568–1575), which he called his masterpiece, with a dome of about 31 metres that he said equalled that of Hagia Sophia.
nodes.src: Sinan, Tezkiretü'l-bünyan; Gülru Necipoğlu, The Age of Sinan (2005); Godfrey Goodwin, Sinan (1993).

nodes.label: İznik and Blue Mosque
nodes.full: The potters of İznik developed a white fritware with a painted underglaze in cobalt blue, turquoise, green and a raised tomato red that gave the court's mosques, notably the Rüstem Pasha Mosque (c. 1561–1563) and the Sultan Ahmed Mosque (1609–1616) with its 20,000 tiles, its colours; the kilns declined from about 1620 as the court's orders fell.
nodes.src: Nurhan Atasoy and Julian Raby, Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey (1989); Necipoğlu 2005.

nodes.label: Fuzuli and Bâkî
nodes.full: Fuzuli of Baghdad (d. 1556), who wrote in Turkish, Persian and Arabic, produced the Leyla and Mecnun, a Turkish mystical love poem; Bâkî (1526–1600), poet of Süleyman's court, was the master of the Ottoman divan poem, in Persian forms and Turkish language, and the Ottoman poets of the age, such as Nev'î and Nef'î, set the classical standard of the literature.
nodes.src: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry vols. 3–4 (1904–1905); Walter Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song (1985).

nodes.label: Evliya Çelebi
nodes.full: Evliya Çelebi (1611–c. 1685), a traveller from a family of the court, wrote in ten volumes the Seyahatname, an account of his journeys from Istanbul to Vienna, the Caucasus, Egypt, Crimea and the Balkans between 1640 and 1680, mixing observation with legend and humour; its descriptions of towns, customs and languages remain a major source for the Ottoman world.
nodes.src: Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname (ed. Dankoff et al.); Robert Dankoff, An Ottoman Mentality (2004).

nodes.label: Miniature and Karagöz
nodes.full: The court painters of the nakkaşhane, among them Nakkaş Osman and Matrakçı Nasuh, produced illustrated histories (the Süleymanname, the Hünername), campaign albums with views of cities and the Surname of 1582 on the circumcision festival of Murad III's son; the shadow theatre Karagöz, with its stock characters, became a popular entertainment.
nodes.src: Esin Atıl, The Age of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (1987); Metin And, Karagöz (1975).

nodes.label: Mustafa Âlî and advice literature
nodes.full: Mustafa Âlî, a bureaucrat and historian of Gallipoli, wrote the Counsel for Sultans (Nushatü's-selâtîn, 1581) and the Künhü'l-ahbar, in which he saw an empire in decline from the time of Süleyman, with corruption in recruitment and promotion; Koçi Bey's treatise to Murad IV (1630) and Katip Çelebi's work of 1653 gave similar diagnoses and the genre of nasihatname, advice for the sultan, developed into a distinct literature.
nodes.src: Mustafa Âlî, Counsel for Sultans (trans. Tietze, 1979); Cornell Fleischer, Bureaucrat and Intellectual (1986); Koçi Bey, Risale (1631).

nodes.label: Taqi al-Din’s observatory
nodes.full: Taqi al-Din al-Rasid, a scholar of astronomy and mechanics from Damascus, was made chief astronomer in 1571 and in 1577 built an observatory at Galata with large instruments, with the support of Sokollu and Murad III; it was demolished in 1580 after a plague, which was seen by its opponents as an effect of looking into the future, and by some modern historians as a result of the death of Sokollu and the hostility of the religious establishment.
nodes.src: Taqi al-Din, Sidrat muntahā al-afkār; Aydın Sayılı, The Observatory in Islam (1960); Ekmeleddin İhsanoğlu (ed.), History of the Ottoman State, Society and Civilisation (2001).

nodes.label: Piri Reis
nodes.full: Piri Reis, a naval captain, drew in 1513 a map of the Atlantic with parts of the American coast based on Columbus, Portuguese and Arab charts, found in the Topkapı in 1929, and in 1521 and 1526 wrote the Kitab-ı Bahriye, a book of the Mediterranean's harbours and sailing directions; he was executed in 1553 after failing at Hormuz.
nodes.src: Topkapı Palace Library, Hazine 1824; Piri Reis, Kitab-ı Bahriye; Svat Soucek, Piri Reis and Turkish Mapmaking (1996).

nodes.label: Katip Çelebi
nodes.full: Katip Çelebi (Hajji Khalifa), a clerk in the army accounts, wrote the Keşfü'z-zünûn, a bibliographic encyclopaedia of some 14,500 titles, the Cihannüma, a geography that used European sources, and the Düstûrü'l-amel on the reform of the finances; his Mîzânü'l-hak (1656) set out the debates between the Kadızadeli and the Sufis from the view of a rationalist.
nodes.src: Katip Çelebi, Keşfü'z-zünûn; Mizan ül-hakk (trans. G. L. Lewis, 1957); Orhan Şaik Gökyay (ed.).

nodes.label: Price revolution
nodes.full: Inflows of silver from the New World through Europe, rising population and the costs of war pushed Ottoman prices up by perhaps 150 per cent from 1580 to 1620; the state's response in 1585–1586 was to debase the akçe by half and so to cut real salaries, a measure that led to the revolt of the Janissaries and cavalry of 1589 and set off a crisis in the finances.
nodes.src: Ömer Lütfi Barkan, ‘The Price Revolution of the Sixteenth Century’, IJMES 6 (1975); Şevket Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000).

nodes.label: Provisioning of Istanbul
nodes.full: The capital, with about 400,000 to 700,000 people in the sixteenth century, was supplied by a managed economy in which the state fixed prices and compelled deliveries of grain, mutton, oil and wood from Thrace, the Black Sea coasts, Egypt and the Danubian principalities, treated the supply as a fiscal and political necessity and punished hoarding.
nodes.src: Robert Mantran, Istanbul dans la seconde moitié du XVIIe siècle (1962); Imber 2002; Suraiya Faroqhi, Subjects of the Sultan (2000).

nodes.label: Coffee, spices and silk
nodes.full: Coffee from Yemen reached Istanbul in the 1550s, the first coffeehouses opening about 1554, and was drunk across the empire; spices came through Cairo, Basra and Aleppo in competition with the Portuguese route round Africa, and the silk of Iran through Aleppo and Bursa to the merchants of Venice, France and England.
nodes.src: Ralph Hattox, Coffee and Coffeehouses (1985); Suraiya Faroqhi 2000; Niels Steensgaard, The Asian Trade Revolution of the Seventeenth Century (1974).

nodes.label: Janissary pay
nodes.full: The Janissary corps grew from some 12,000 men in the 1560s to over 35,000 by 1650 and received daily wages in debased coin, with the practice of paying them from the new taxes; the corps' interest as a privileged group of the capital in the offices and trades turned the army into a political force in the 1620s.
nodes.src: Kunt 1983; Murphey 1999; Tezcan 2010.

nodes.label: Sinan’s waterworks and mosques
nodes.full: Sinan built or restored the water system of Istanbul, the Kırkçeşme aqueduct, with the Mağlova viaduct (1563) and the Büyükçekmece bridge of four spans (1567), and the bridges at Drina (Višegrad), and the great arched viaducts of Thrace; the aqueduct ran for 55 kilometres and fed mosques, fountains and public baths.
nodes.src: Necipoğlu 2005; Goodwin 1993; Kâzım Çeçen, Sinan Devrinde İstanbul Suyolları (1988).

nodes.label: Arsenal and guns
nodes.full: The imperial foundry at Tophane in Istanbul cast bronze guns of enormous bore, up to the great Dardanelles guns, and the Ottoman army had a corps of artillerymen (topçu) and wagoners (top arabacı) numbered in thousands; the Ottomans were among the first states to use handguns across a whole infantry corps, and their siege trains made possible the conquest of Rhodes, Belgrade and Buda.
nodes.src: Ágoston 2005; Murphey 1999.

nodes.label: Galley and galleon
nodes.full: The Ottoman fleet, based on galleys with oars and a few guns, was rebuilt at the Arsenal to some 200 ships after Lepanto but, though able to take Crete, it was left behind by the Atlantic powers' sailing ships carrying broadside guns, which reached the Mediterranean in the 1590s; the Ottomans adopted the galleon only in the later seventeenth century.
nodes.src: Imber 2002; Palmira Brummett 1994; Idris Bostan, Osmanlı Bahriye Teşkilatı (1992).

nodes.label: Franco-Ottoman alliance
nodes.full: After the defeat of Francis I at Pavia in 1525, France and the Ottomans made an informal alliance against Charles V: the French ambassador Jean de La Forêt negotiated in 1536, the Ottoman fleet under Barbarossa wintered at Toulon in 1543–1544 and helped to take Nice, and the alliance, a cause of scandal in Christian Europe, lasted with interruptions until the French Revolution.
nodes.src: Christine Isom-Verhaaren, Allies with the Infidel (2011); Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Indian Ocean expeditions
nodes.full: An Ottoman fleet from Suez under Hadım Süleyman Pasha took Aden in 1538 and besieged the Portuguese at Diu, and in the 1550s Piri Reis and Seydi Ali Reis led expeditions to Hormuz and the Gulf; in 1565 an Ottoman mission went to the sultan of Aceh. The effort to dislodge the Portuguese failed but gave the empire the Red Sea coast, Yemen and Basra.
nodes.src: Salih Özbaran, The Ottoman Response to European Expansion (1994); Giancarlo Casale, The Ottoman Age of Exploration (2010).

nodes.label: English and Dutch companies
nodes.full: Queen Elizabeth sought an alliance against Spain and obtained capitulations for the English in 1580–1581, and the Levant Company was founded in 1592; the Dutch received the capitulation in 1612, and the competition of the Atlantic merchants with the French and the Venetians for the markets of the Levant shaped the trade of the seventeenth century.
nodes.src: Susan Skilliter, William Harborne and the Trade with Turkey (1977); van den Boogert 2005.

nodes.label: Zsitvatorok
nodes.full: The treaty ending the Long War was negotiated at the mouth of the Zsitva river with no tribute, with the emperor named padishah and not just king (kıral), a lump sum of 200,000 florins and equal footing in diplomatic form; the first treaty in which the sultan accepted the emperor as an equal and not as a tributary.
nodes.src: Treaty of Zsitvatorok (1606); Imber 2002; Murphey 1999.

nodes.label: Little Ice Age
nodes.full: Tree-ring and documentary evidence show a run of extremely cold winters and severe drought in Anatolia in the 1590s and 1600s, with crop failures, loss of flocks and migration of peasants to the cities, and some historians have linked it to the Jelali rebellions; others emphasise the government's military and fiscal policies.
nodes.src: Sam White, The Climate of Rebellion in the Early Modern Ottoman Empire (2011); Griswold 1983.

nodes.label: Population growth
nodes.full: The surveys show the number of households in Anatolia and Rumelia rising by 40 to 70 per cent between 1520 and 1580, with a total population of the empire of perhaps 25 to 30 million by 1600; the pressure on land, the rise of landless men (levend) and the growth of cities such as Istanbul, Edirne and Aleppo form part of the background to the Jelali revolts.
nodes.src: Barkan 1957; Imber 2002; Faroqhi 2000.

nodes.label: Plague and fires
nodes.full: Plague recurred in the capital and the ports every 10–15 years, with outbreaks in 1573–1574, 1592 and 1625–1627 among others, and Istanbul's timber houses burnt in great fires, as in 1660 when much of the city was destroyed; the city's authorities responded with relief, burial and the removal of the court to Edirne, but not with quarantine until the nineteenth century.
nodes.src: Nükhet Varlık, Plague and Empire in the Early Modern Mediterranean World (2015); Mantran 1962.

nodes.label: Women before the kadi
nodes.full: The records of the kadi courts of Kayseri, Aintab, Bursa and elsewhere show women, Muslim and non-Muslim, suing for dower, inheritance and divorce, buying and selling property and endowing waqfs, and appearing in person or through representatives; the shares of women in the property of waqfs of the sixteenth century were large, and the sources show women as economic agents more than the legal rules might suggest.
nodes.src: Ronald Jennings, ‘Women in the Early 17th Century Ottoman Judicial Records’, JESHO 18 (1975); Haim Gerber, State, Society, and Law in Islam (1994); Leslie Peirce, Morality Tales (2003).

nodes.label: Eunuchs
nodes.full: The black eunuchs of the harem, brought from Ethiopia and the Sudan, and the white eunuchs of the inner service, who were mostly Circassians, Georgians and Balkans boys, held posts that ran from the guarding of the women to the management of the endowments of the holy cities; the chief black eunuch, the Kızlar Ağası, became one of the most powerful people at court from the 1590s.
nodes.src: Peirce 1993; Jane Hathaway, Beshir Agha (2006).

nodes.label: Non-Muslim subjects
nodes.full: Non-Muslims paid the poll tax (cizye) and could not build new churches without permission or bear arms, but ran their own courts of personal law, and in Istanbul, Salonica, Aleppo and Izmir ran much of the banking and long-distance trade; the sultan's physicians, translators and dragomans came from these communities, and the Phanar, the Greek quarter of Istanbul, became a source of Greek officials in the later seventeenth century.
nodes.src: Braude and Lewis 1982; Shaw 1991; Runciman 1968.

nodes.label: Janissary and villager
nodes.full: By the early seventeenth century Janissaries were allowed to marry, to enrol their sons and to trade in the city, and were in effect part of its craft and market life, with garrisons in provincial towns holding local property; villagers, their taxes shifted from the old rates to cash and avarız, left the land for the towns in the Jelali years or took service as armed bands.
nodes.src: Kunt 1983; Tezcan 2010; Faroqhi 2000.

nodes.label: The conquest of the Mamluk lands
nodes.full: Selim I’s victories at Marj Dabiq and Ridaniya in 1516–1517 brought Syria, Egypt and the Hijaz under Ottoman rule and made the sultan protector of Mecca and Medina.
nodes.src: background — see the Ottoman Empire 1299–1517 folio (ottoman-empire-1299-1517)

nodes.label: The Safavid challenge after Chaldiran
nodes.full: After the defeat at Chaldiran in 1514 the Safavid shahs remained the Ottomans’ rival and the patrons of the Shia Qizilbash, and the frontier in Iraq, the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia was contested for two centuries.
